Since that time, he has had pain and loss of hearing in his right ear. On arrival, he is in mild distress. Exami nation shows abras ions over the right side of the face, neck, and upper chest. There is blood in the external auditory canal of the right ear and swell ing and ecchymosis of the right pinna. correctExplanation: The tympanic membrane separates the externa l and middle ear and is important for the conductance and amplification of auditory vibrations. The tympanic membrane may be ruptured by blunt trauma to the externa l ear, by perforation with a cotton tipped swab, or by barotrauma, which most commonly occurs as a result of concussive blast injury (as in this case) or rapid ascent during diving. Patients may experience ipsilatera l conductive hearing loss, ear pain, tinnitus, vertigo, or ipsilatera l facia l weakness caused by injury of the facial nerve. Patients should undergo an urgent examination to detect other cranial injuries, spinal injuries, or basilar skull fractures, along with evaluation for barotrauma involving other susceptible organ systems such as the respiratory system (pneumothorax) and the gastrointestina l tract (hollow viscus perforation). Initial management includes antibiotic ear drops, audiology, and referral to an otolaryngologist. Patients with severe conductive hearing loss often require surgical repair.

Fracture of the temporal bone (Choice A) is a type of basilar skull fracture that may lead to conductive hearing loss caused by injury to the ossicles or tympanic membrane. Basilar skull fracture is typica lly accompanied by other clinical signs and symptoms including hemotympanum and Battle sign (retroauricular ecchymosis). Injury to the air cells of the mastoid process (Choice B) typical ly occurs in the setting of mastoiditis. Mastoiditis presents with otalgia and retroauricular edema and erythema, and often follows a midd le ear infection. Pressure on the vestibu locochlear nerve (Choice C) presents with sensorineural hearing loss and is often accompanied by tinnitus, vertigo, and nystagmus. He and his friend had been fishing on a small boat wh,en the patient's symptoms began. The patient had been operating the outboard motor continuously for the latter part of the day. correctExplanation: The patient is presenting with signs and symptoms concerning for carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning and should be treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy. CO has a significantly higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen and binds to available hemoglobin. On binding, CO displaces oxygen from heme, limiting total carrying capacity, and results in maintenance of hemoglobin in the relaxed form, with loss of cooperative binding. This results in systemic hypoxemia and tissue hypoxia. Risk factors include prolonged exposure to motor vehicle exhaust (as in operating an outboard motor for an extended period of time); exposure to byproducts of burning charcoal, gas, or petroleum (especially in poorly ventilated areas); or exposure to paint thinners that contain methylene chloride (which is metabolized to CO). Symptoms include headache, light-headedness, nausea, and altered mental status. Patients typically have a paradoxically normal peripheral oxygen saturation and may display tachycardia, tachypnea, and cherry-red skin on physical examination in the late stages of CO poisoning. Acute management involves removing the patient from the exposure and treatment with 100% supplemental oxygen to displace CO from hemoglobin. Severe cases and high-risk patients demonstrating any degree of neurologic deficit or significant end-organ dysfunction should be treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy. CO also binds cytochrome complexes and disrupts the electron transport chain; the resultant cellular dysfunction is best addressed with hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after she fell off a sailboat into a freshwater lake. A witness reported that she was under water for approximate ly 2 minutes; when she was rescued, she was cyanotic and unresponsive. After initial mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, she began cough ing and breathing again , and her color returned . On arrival in the emergency department , the patient is awake and alert. She has mild shortness of breath and a cough. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 93/45 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 94%. Auscu ltation of the lungs discloses mild wheezes. There are no signs of external trauma. A chest x-ray shows mild diffuse interstitial markings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctExplanation: Admission to the hospital for observation is the most appropriate management for this young girl who recently suffered a nonfatal drowning incident. Unexpected submersion in water leads to reflexive breath holding followed by air hunger and an eventua l reflexive inspiratory effort. This leads to hypoxia through either aspiration of water or laryngospasm when water contacts the vocal cords. Prolonged hypoxemia leads to end-organ dysfunction including acidosis, hypoxic brain injury, and cardiac arrhythmias. Exposure of the alveoli to water can lead to the development of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which appears on chest imaging as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. ARDS can develop immediate ly after injury or slowly over many hours and can be rapidly fatal. In general, all nonfata l drowning victims with any degree of hypoxia, respiratory distress, or infiltrates on imaging should be hospitalized to monitor for the evidence of the development of ARDS and complications of drowning.

Antibiotics are reserved for patients with presumed or proven bacterial infections, but drowning does not necessari ly predispose to the development of bacterial infection. Corticosteroid therapy (Choice C) is not useful in the management of drowning victims. It is more commonly used for shortness of breath in the setting of asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and croup. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 60-year-o ld Hispanic woman is brought to the emergency department by her son because of a 1-week history of cough and low-grade fever. She understands some English but does not speak it fluently. Her son speaks fluent English and Spanish. The physician is not fluent in Spanish but can communicate limitedly with the patient. Her temperatu re is 37.8°C (100°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturat ion of 98%. Breath sounds are decreased at the lung bases with occasional rhonchi that clear with cough. An x-ray of the chest shows no evidence of pneumonia; howeve r, a 1-cm mass that requires follow­ up is noted in the left lower lobe. An ECG shows normal sinus rhythm and no evidence of ischemic changes. The patient is anxious to leave, and the hospita l interpreter is with another patient. Which of the following is the most appropr iate way to communicate the need for further evaluation of a potential malignancy?

choices.A: Ask the son to translate the discharge instructions to the patient
choices.B: Call the patient's primary care physician to communicate the information
choices.C: Give the discharge instructions directly to the son
choices.D: Wait for the interpreter before issuing the discharge instructions
choices.E: Write down the discharge instructions in English and ask the patient to give them to her primary care physician

correctExplanation: Waiting for the interpreter before issuing the discharge instructions is the appropriate action in this scenario. Professional interpreters can provide high-quality translations that maintain patient safety. Credentialed interpreters are trained in medical knowledge and vocabulary, ethics, and cultural sensitivity. Relying on a family member for interpreting increases the risk for miscommunication about medical or culturally relevant details and can jeopardize informed consent for treatment and patient safety. This is important for all care, but particularly so in this case because a miscommunication could jeopardize a timely diagnosis of malignancy in this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Asking the son to translate the discharge instructions to the patient (Choice A) or giving the discharge instructions directly to the son (Choice C) are not appropriate. Family members should not act as interpreters for patients. The nuances of a medical situation may be misunderstood by an untrained interpreter and therefore miscommunicated to the patient. The only situation in which interpretation by a family member is acceptable is an emergency when no other option exists. Calling the patient's primary care physician to communicate the information (Choice B) or writing down the discharge instructions in English and asking the patient to give them to her primary care physician (Choice E) are both inappropriate because they displace the responsibility of the patient's care onto someone else. While the patient's primary care provider should be notified of the patient's visit and the need for malignancy work-up, the burden of sharing this with the patient is the responsibi lity of the emergency department physician via a professional interpreter. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

Acute appendicitis typical ly presents with abdomina l pain that is often periumbi lical at onset and which may later migrate to the right lower quadrant, along with leukocytosis and tenderness to palpation. Patients often develop fever and may also experience nausea and anorexia. Other genitourinary, vascular, muscu loskeletal, and gastrointestina l mimics should be excluded. The diagnosis can be confirmed with CT scan, MRI, or ultrasonography. Appendectomy is indicated to prevent appendicea l rupture, which can lead to peritonitis or an intra-abdominal abscess. Patients classically present with acute onset pelvic or lower abdominal pain, nausea, emesis, and an adnexal mass or tenderness on pelvic examination. Ovarian torsion is a surgical emergency and requires detorsion to preserve the ovary once the diagnosis is made.

questionStem: A 48-year-o ld woman comes to the emergency department 9 hours after she was bitten on the right forearm by another woman during an altercation in a bar. Medical history is unremarkable and the patient takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examinat ion shows a 1-cm avulsion injury to the right forearm. correctExplanation: The appropriate first step in management of a human bite is irrigation and antibiotic therapy. Human bites that penetrate the skin are at high risk for becoming infected with oral and skin flora, including Eikenel/a, Fusobacterium , Staphylococcus, and Streptococcus species. Viral pathogens such as herpes simplex virus and HIV can also be transmitted. Superficial infection presents as cellulitis with tenderness, warmth, and erythema, but deeper infection can occur, which may present with pain with passive movement, crepitus, and systemic illness. This patient does not yet demonstrate any signs of infection. In this case, wound management including irrigation, control of bleeding, and remova l of any visible debris should be performed. The wounds should not be closed because this increases the risk for infection. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis is appropriate, particular ly in patients with wounds on the hands or face, if the patient is immunocompromised, or if the patient has a prosthetic valve, prosthetic joint, or vascular graft. The preferred empiric antibiotic is amoxicil lin-clavu lanate, which covers both oral and skin flora.

The wounds should instead be left to heal by secondary intention. The exception is for bites on the face, which is a more sensitive cosmetic area. questionStem: A previous ly healthy 42-yea r-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after the onset of generalized weakness, shortness of breath , severe abdomina l cramps, and sweating that began while he was gardening. His temperatu re is 37.3°C (99.2°F), pulse is 52/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Examination shows diaphoresis , excessive lacrimation, and 2-mm pupils that are reactive to light. Diffuse wheezes are heard on auscultation. Abdomina l examination shows no tenderness. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the extremities with prominent muscle fascicu lations. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+. Babinski sign is absent. Sensat ion is intact. correctExplanation: Symptoms of organophosphate poisoning are caused by increased concentrations of acetylcholine in the neuronal junction caused by the irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase. Organophosphates are present in pesticides and patients can be exposed through absorption, inhalation, or ingestion. Symptoms of cholinergic toxicity secondary to organophosphate poisoning included diarrhea, vomiting, excessive urination, lethargy, and altered mental status. Physical examination may demonstrate bradycardia, hypotension, miosis, increased salivation or tearing, diaphoresis, and evidence of bronchospasm. Muscle weakness and paralysis may be present, in addition to cardiac arrhythmias and respiratory failure. Long-term complications include neurocognitive deficits. Treatment consists of decontamination (eg, removal of contaminated clothing), fluid resuscitation, endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation if indicated, and administration of atropine. Atropine acts by competitive ly binding the acetylcho line receptors, which prevents the cholinergic effects of acetylcholine. Pralidoxime is used in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning and exerts its effects at the neuromuscular junction, where atropine is ineffective, by reactivating cholinesterase. Benzodiazepines may be administered if affected patients are convulsing.

correctExplanation: Women of reproductive age presenting for care because of pelvic pain or abdominal cramping should be evaluated for pregnancy with a measurement of serum ~-human chorionic gonadotropin (~-hCG) concentration. Pregnancy is suspected when there is a missed or delayed menstrual period. Ectopic pregnancy is an abnormal pregnancy in which the fertilized ovum implants in the fallopian tube (most common), on the ovary, within the peritoneal cavity, or in any nonendometrial location. It often causes symptoms early in pregnancy because of the restricted area for fetal development and commonly presents with lower abdomina l or pelvic pain and vaginal bleeding. Physical examination may disclose adnexal tenderness on the side of implantation. ~-hCG is produced by the placenta, is undetectable in the serum of nonpregnant patients, and doubles approximately every 48 hours during an early normal pregnancy. ~-hCG concentrations do not increase as expected in ectopic pregnancy, often lagging the normal expected doubling. Treatment of an ectopic pregnancy can be medical, using methotrexate for small, early pregnancies, but may require salpingectomy or evacuation with laparoscopy for larger pregnancies or in cases of medical treatment failure. Complications of ectopic pregnancy include rupture, bleeding, and hemoperitoneum.

While some postpartum vaginal bleeding can persist for up to 8 weeks following delivery, late or secondary postpartum hemorrhage occurs more than 24 hours after delivery and is characterized by significant uterine bleeding, such as the passage of clots or bleeding that soaks a menstrual pad in less than 1 hour. A common cause of secondary postpartum hemorrhage is retained products of conception, which can become infected and cause a postpartum endometritis. Endometritis presents with fever, tachycardia, abdominal pain, uterine tenderness, and leukocytosis, as in this patient. Ultrasonography can identify the retained products of conception by disclosing echogenic material in the uterine cavity. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after collapsing near the completion of a 26-mile run in warm, humid weather. On arrival, he is obtunded and warm. correctExplanation: Heat stroke is characterized by an increased body temperature that occurs when the body is exposed to high environmental temperatures and high humidity, and it commonly occurs in young athletes or in elderly patients with impaired thermoregulatory capacity. Excessive heat exposure and increased core body temperature leads to cardiovascular and neurologic dysfunction with secondary tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension. Vasodilation of superficia l blood vessels may lead to multi-organ system failure, including hepatic and renal ischemia, rhabdomyo lysis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment includes cooling of the patient with fans or ice water, continuous core temperature monitoring, and support of airway, breathing, and circulation. questionStem: A 60-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment because of a 12-hour history of moderate, diffuse abdominal pain and vomiting. Two weeks ago, she underwe nt a sigmoidectomy for perforated diverticulitis. Her postoperative course has been otherwise uncomplicated. She has not had fever, diarrhea, or pain with urination. Her last bowel movement yesterday was normal. She has not passed any flatus today. Her medications are ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and oxycodone-acetaminophen. On arrival, the patient is in moderate distress. She is awake and alert. Her temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F), pulse is 100/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 140/65 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 98%. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnorma lities. The abdomen is moderately distended and diffusely tender to palpation in all four quadrants. The surgical incision is clean, dry, and intact. Bowel sounds are decreased. An x-ray of the abdomen shows multiple loops of distended small bowel with air-fluid levels throughout; no air is noted in the rectum. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Bowel obstruction is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with previous abdominal surgery presenting with abdominal pain and obstipation. Obstruction of the bowel occurs from partial or complete blockage of the bowel lumen and typically presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Partial obstruction allows a degree of continued flatus with diminished stooling, and complete obstruction will result in obstipation (no passage of stool or flatus). Obstruction has many potential causes, although the most common are postsurgical peritoneal adhesions and hernias. On physical examination, patients typically present with abdominal tenderness, distention, tympany to percussion, and borborygmi (high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds). Potential complications include bowel rupture and necrosis, which can result in sudden-onset peritoneal signs such as rebound tenderness and guarding. X-ray of the abdomen typically discloses multiple air-fluid levels in the setting of dilated bowel loops. Management requires bowel rest, insertion of a nasogastric tube for decompression, and intravenous hydration followed by surgical intervention if the obstruction does not autoreduce. Partial obstruction may resolve with monitoring, supportive care, and bowel rest, whereas complete obstruction or any complicated partial obstruction generally requires management through exploratory laparotomy.

questionStem: A 68-year-o ld man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of abdom inal cramps after eating. He has also noticed a 2.3- kg (5-lb) weight loss during this time. He has had occasional loose stools but does not report any blood. He has hypertension and congestive heart failure. Medications are metopro lol, digoxin, and amlodipine. His medical records from 6 months ago show a left ventricu lar ejection fraction of 20%. He has no known drug allergies. On arrival, he appears thin and uncomfortable. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 138/72 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 97%. Cardiopu lmonary examination discloses an S3 and bilateral basilar crackles. The abdomen is soft with minimal genera lized tenderness to palpation. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?

choices.E: Upper gastrointest inal series with small bowel follow through

correctExplanation: CT angiography is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), recent weight loss, and postprandial abdominal pain most likely has nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia. Mesenteric ischemia can occur secondary to thrombosis of the mesenteric artery or can result from low-flow cardiac states leading to intestinal hypoperfusion. The blood supply to the intestines is primarily derived from the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA). Following a meal, the blood flow to the intestines increases to aid in the digestive process. In nonocclusive mesenteric ischemia, constriction of the mesenteric artery in combination with a decreased cardiac output leads to a supply-demand mismatch and subsequent intestina l ischemia. This is often experienced as postprandia l pain which may make some patients avoid eating altogether, thereby leading to weight loss. The diagnosis is made by CT angiography, which shows narrowing of the mesenteric vessels and their branches. When the condition is secondary to HFrEF, therapy is aimed at improving cardiac function.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abdomina l ultrasonography (Choice A) can be used to evaluate the abdominal aorta and flow through its main branches, which include the SMA, IMA, and celiac trunk, but advanced cross-sectional imaging with CT angiography is more sensitive and specific for mesenteric ischemia. Barium enema (Choice B) is used infrequent ly in current clinical practice, but it can occasionally help to diagnose malrotation or volvulus. It is not helpful in the diagnosis of mesenteric ischemia. - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 54-year-o ld man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his wife found him lying unresponsive on the bed. His fingerstick blood glucose concentration was 20 mg/dl (1.11 mmol/L), so she called 911. His medicat ions are glimepiride and metformin. He has no known drug allergies. At the scene, paramedics could not obtain intravenous access and transported him to the hospita l. On arrival, the patient is diaphoretic and moaning softly. He does not cooperate w ith the examination. His temperature is 34.8°C (94.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 8/min, and blood pressure is 134/86 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%. Cardiopu lmonary examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. No skin rashes are noted. Now, fingerstick blood glucose concentration is 15 mg/dl (0.83 mmol/L). The nurses continue to have difficulty obtaining intravenous access. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management while awaiting intravenous access?
correctExplanation: Intramuscular administration of glucagon is the most appropriate step in management of this diabetic patient with severe hypoglycemia and no intravenous access. The treatment of severe hypoglycemia in a diabetic patient requires administration of either carbohydrates or glucagon. If intravenous access is available, carbohydrates can easily be given as 50% dextrose. However, in this case, intramuscular glucagon is a fast and safe way to reverse hypoglycemia in a patient with impaired consciousness and no intravenous access. After administration of glucagon, the patient must be closely monitored and intravenous access obtained because the effect of glucagon is transient. After intravenous access is available, a continuous infusion of glucose will likely be necessary. Any patient with hypoglycemia taking long-acting oral hypoglycemics ( sulfonylureas in this case) requires prolonged monitoring or admission because rebound hypoglycemia is common.

Any delay of glucagon administration in this patient will increase his chances of death. While the patient's respiratory rate is low, bag-valve-mask ventilation (Choice B) is not necessary at this time given the adequate oxygen saturation of 96%. It is more important to address the underlying cause of this patient's symptoms, which is severe hypoglycemia. -- - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - - - - - r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old man is brought to the emergency department by paramed ics 15 minutes after he was involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. The patient was traveling at about 5 miles per hour (8 km/hr) in a parking lot when his car struck a parked vehicle. Paramedics say that the damage to both vehicles was minimal. The, patient says he consumed two beers earlier in the evening. On arrival, he is awake, alert, and fully oriented. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows tenderness and swelling of the right elbow but no other abnormal ities. The physician recomme nds that an x-ray of the elbow be performed. The patient says that he would prefer to leave; he is able to verba lize the risks of leaving using his own words. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in manageme nt?

choices.A: Allow the patient to leave against medica l advice
choices.C: Detain the patient until his blood alcohol concentratio n is measured
choices.D: Discharge the patient with a diagnosis of elbow contusion
choices.E: Obtain x-rays despite the patient's wishes

correctExplanation: Patient autonomy is one of four common medical ethical principles, along with beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. Autonomy posits that patients have the right to make their decisions provided that they have the capacity to do so and that they have been provided with appropriate information for use in making such a decision. A consenting adult with decision-making capacity has the right to refuse some or all aspects of medical care even if such a decision may result in short- or long-term morbidity or mortality. In this case, the patient is declining further work-up and treatment of a musculoskeleta l injury induced by a motor vehicle collision. Provided that this patient has capacity and that the caring physician has explained the benefits, risks, and alternatives of not performing the x-ray of the elbow, the patient may elect to refuse and then be allowed to leave against medical advice.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. It is not necessary to call the police (Choice B) in this case because the patient has demonstrated lawful behavior in the emergency department since arrival. It is not the physician's role to determine whether the police need to be involved in the motor vehicle collision, and disclosing such would be a breach of patient privacy. If the patient had assaulted providers who wished to pursue legal action, or if he had committed a reportable offense (eg, discharged a firearm), calling the police may be appropriate. Detaining the patient until his blood alcohol concentration is measured (Choice C) or obtaining x-rays despite the patient's wishes (Choice E) violates the ethical principle of patient autonomy. Because this patient demonstrates decision-making capacity by being able to verbalize the risks of leaving in his own words (and is not suspected to be impaired), there is no justification to detain the patient or perform tests against his will. r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after losing consciousness while eating at home. It is general ly acute in onset following a specific exposure and general ly does not self-resolve. If not managed promptly, death can occur from hypoxia and/or distributive shock. Anaphylaxis is a form of distributive shock, which is characterized by a primary reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This reduction in SVR is secondary to lgE-mediated histamine and cytokine release. Cardiac output increases to compensate for low SVR in the early stages of distributive shock. If the inciting state is not appropriate ly treated, further decompensation can occur, resulting in progressive hypotension and insufficient perfusion with associated end-organ damage. After the administration of epinephrine, fluid resuscitation should be initiated to increase intravascular volume to support adequate organ perfusion.

Acute serum sickness (Choice A) is a type Ill (immune complex-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction in which antibodies to foreign proteins are produced and immune complexes deposit in membranes, leading to tissue damage. It typically presents with fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and lymphadenopathy 5 to 10 days after exposure. Anaphylaxis is typica lly an immediate and acute reaction. Cardiogenic shock (Choice C) can occur in diseases such as myocarditis, acute myocardial infarction, and congestive heart failure.
